blocks.x: In college, I was introduced to the world of rice cookers when my roommate bought one for our house. I didn't fully realize how spoiled I'd been until we graduated and she moved across the country, taking her rice cooker with her. I was left to make do with the finicky stovetop method that never turned out quite right.

In the years since, I've never been without one. Having consistently fluffy, well-cooked rice means I can turn my attention to the other components of the meal, and that convenience is well worth the price tag and the extra storage space a rice cooker comes with. Besides, there's nothing as humbling as cooking a big pot of rice for company only to find it's turned into a pile of mush.
Our top picks

The best rice cookers are like a kitchen cheat code, a helping hand that ensures at least one part of your meal goes off without a hitch. But they vary a lot in performance. I've tested 41 rice cookers and cooked over 120 cups of rice (and that's just in the Test Kitchen), so I'm here to give you the lowdown and help you choose the right one for your lifestyle, budget, and household size.

I believe the best rice cooker for your money is the Hamilton Beach 7-Cup Digital Programmable Rice Cooker. It's the right size for most people (making up to 14 cups of cooked rice), and at $70 it's a great price. But I also have picks for PFAS-free options, small cookers for tiny spaces, and the Zojirushi NP-HCC10 that makes the absolute best rice, as long as you're willing to pay for it. We think it's worth it.

New in this update: I tested the GreenPan Advanced 8-Cup (Cooked) Rice Cooker and found it to be a good option for those looking for a small rice cooker with a ceramic, PFAS-free nonstick inner pot. I also tested the new KitchenAid Compact Grain and Rice Cooker, but didn't think its performance merited its price tag.
Best rice cooker for most people: Hamilton Beach Digital Programmable Rice Cooker

Capacity: 7 cups (uncooked rice)
Dimensions: (W x D x H) 10.75" x 10.75" x 11"
Weight: 4.8 lb.
Warranty: One-year limited warranty
Features: Delay cook, automatic keep-warm function
Menu settings: white rice, quick rice, whole grain, hot cereals, steam cook, heat/simmer

You don’t need to spend hundreds of dollars to make great rice. The Hamilton Beach Digital Programmable Rice Cooker has consistently impressed me throughout years of testing, and at under $70, I think it’s the best option for most home cooks.

What I love: The Hamilton Beach ranked right behind the Zojirushi (our splurge pick below) in a side-by-side blind tasting of white rice. It excelled in the brown rice test, producing individual and intact grains that had a satisfying amount of bite to them (though if you prefer your brown rice on the softer side, I'd recommend adding a bit more water than the recommended amount). It also fared well with long-grain basmati, producing a pot of fluffy rice on par with (if not better than) some of the more expensive cookers I tested. It cooked each pot of rice significantly faster than the Zojirushi, too: 35 minutes for a pot of white rice as opposed to the Zojirushi’s 50, and an hour for brown rice as opposed to 90 minutes.

But what I really loved about the Hamilton Beach is that despite its low price tag, it doesn't sacrifice some of the helpful features the more high-end cookers tend to have. Besides a standard Keep Warm function, there are also six presets to choose from (white rice, quick rice, whole grain, heat/simmer, steam cook, and hot cereals), a handy delayed start feature (great if you want to prep a pot of rice before work and have it ready by the time you get home in the evening), a cook time countdown, and an audible beep when the rice is done cooking—all things most other options at this price point lack. Its 7-cup (uncooked) capacity is also larger than that of many of the other rice cookers I tested, but the machine's footprint is comparably compact. It's also technically a multi-cooker thanks to the heat/simmer and steam cook settings, though I was primarily interested in its rice-making capabilities for this review and will not vouch for those other functions here.

I named the Hamilton Beach our budget pick two years ago, but after continuing to test it against the previous overall winner and countless other new-to-me models over the past couple of years while watching the price of the Zojirushi climb closer to—and oftentimes above—$400, I can confidently say that it’s the best choice for most home cooks for its balance of performance, features, and affordability.

What I'd leave: While I found the Hamilton Beach to be well-made for a $70-ish machine, it didn’t feel quite as sturdy as the higher-end models we tested. I also didn’t love the design of the lid: It requires you to press and hold a button while manually opening it, and it opens sideways rather than front to back. The inner pot is also relatively thin, which contributed to a scorched layer of rice at the bottom in some of my tests—something that wasn’t a deal-breaker for me in the end but is worth noting. And, unlike many other models we tested, there is no differentiation in the recommended amount of water for different types of rice. I didn’t find that this negatively impacted the resulting rice, though the brown rice, which had a nice bite to it, could be a tad al dente for some with the recommended amount of water.
